title: Vitruvius sand-test register with shared mortar judgment and use scope
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED, NOT SELECTED. Vitruvius De architectura II.4 introduces a sand sample and applies two distinct observations to it: a grating sound when rubbed identifies the best sand, while an earthy sample that leaves only a removable stain or particles on white cloth is still fit for mortar. The same source then changes the result by application context: sea sand is unsuitable for heavily loaded or vaulted walls, old pit sand loses binding, and the pit/river distinction matters for mortar versus plaster. A finite constructor therefore shares one FIT_MORTAR judgment across two tests but preserves use-specific scope.

source.work: Vitruvius, De architectura, Book II, chapter 4
source.source_span: Complete chapter II.4: sand types and two suitability observations; river/sifted-gravel/sea fallback; sea-sand drying and load/vault restrictions; new pit sand and salt/plaster caveat; aged sand loss of binding; pit versus river application contexts.
source.provenance: The LacusCurtius English translation and Latin.it text were used as primary navigation witnesses. The wording around new pit sand and plaster is retained as a source/translation caveat rather than silently normalized. No target language or manuscript Vorlage is claimed.

duplicate_screen.checked: IDEA000394 Vitruvius clock constructor; IDEA000457 Palladius soil probes; IDEA000425 Cato propagation; existing Hero material tests; geometry and source-only material cards returned by route-check.
duplicate_screen.difference: The Palladius card classifies soil by a pit residual and taste axis. This Vitruvius card requires two different observations to converge on one mortar-suitability judgment, then scopes that judgment by construction use and sand age. It is not a generic input classifier or a clock/mechanism writer.

presuppositions: A SAND_SAMPLE is introduced before its color, texture, rubbing, cloth, age, and source-location observations.
FIT_MORTAR, BEST_SAND, FIT_PLASTER, and FIT_HEAVY_OR_VAULTED_WALL are distinct typed judgments; one does not imply all others.
The source's two early observations can converge on mortar suitability even though one identifies best quality and the other accepts an earthy but usable sample.
Sea-sand and aged-sand restrictions are application/age conditions, not new sand identities.
The translation's pit-sand/plaster wording is retained as unresolved source scope where the accessible English text is internally awkward.

clauses.content: For rubble walls, first determine sand fit for lime and free from earth; the named colors are black, white, deep red, and bright red.
Among the named sorts, the best is the sample that makes a grating sound when rubbed between the fingers.
An earthy sample lacking the named roughness is nevertheless fit if it leaves only a stain or earth particles on white cloth that can easily be brushed away.
If no sand pits exist, use river sand or sifted gravel; sea sand is a fallback but dries slowly.
Walls using sea sand should not be heavily loaded unless built in small portions; sea sand is not fit for walls intended to receive vaulting.

The chapter retains its salt/plaster warning and then says fresh pit or river contexts behave differently; the accessible translation's repeated pit-sand wording is kept as a source ambiguity rather than repaired.
Sand dug long ago and exposed to sun, moon, and rain loses binding, cannot hold rubble stones against sliding, and is unfit for walls supporting great weights.
Pit sand is excellent for mortar but unfit for plaster because its strength causes cracking; river sand, when beaten, makes hard plaster like cement.

complete_examples.reference_resolution: The same introduced S1 carries the rubbing observation into the mortar-use judgment; no second sample is invented.
S2 reaches the same mortar judgment through the cloth test while retaining its earthy quality; it is not silently upgraded to BEST_SAND.
The same general suitability question is narrowed by the use register; sea-sand fallback does not license vaulted walls.
Age and application scope override an earlier generic mortar suitability; the sample identity remains S4.

global_rules: RUB(S1) with GRATING_SOUND yields BEST_SAND and FIT_MORTAR; BEST_SAND is stronger than the generic fit judgment.
CLOTH_SHAKE(S2) with only REMOVABLE_STAIN_OR_PARTICLES yields FIT_MORTAR while preserving EARTHY quality; it does not yield BEST_SAND.
SEA_SAND is a fallback source with DRIES_SLOWLY and is rejected for VAULTING_WALL or heavy load unless the source's small-portion condition is retained.
OLD_EXPOSED sand loses binding and is rejected for HEAVY_LOAD_WALL even if a different earlier test made fresh material fit for mortar.
PIT_SAND and RIVER_SAND have distinct application rules for mortar and plaster; the accessible translation's awkward salt/plaster wording remains a caveat, not a free branch.
Every later reference to a sample resolves to the locally introduced SAND_SAMPLE register; a new sample requires an explicit INTRODUCE operation.
constructor.observable_consequence: Two different observation methods converge on FIT_MORTAR while preserving a quality distinction; later source context changes the complete judgment without changing sample identity. An all-tests-equal or all-uses-fit rival cannot retain both convergence and the sea/age/use restrictions.

rivals.R_ONE_TEST: Only grating sound is meaningful; the cloth example cannot produce the source's shared FIT_MORTAR judgment.
rivals.R_ALL_USES_FIT: Any sand fit for mortar is automatically fit for plaster, vaulting, and heavy walls; this loses the source's application scope.
rivals.R_NEW_SAMPLE_ON_SCOPE: Every later application clause creates a new material instead of updating the locally introduced sample's age/use state.

falsifier: Reject the constructor if the complete chapter cannot preserve both mortar-converging tests, the distinct BEST versus FIT quality, the sea-sand/vault restrictions, the aged-sand loss of binding, and the pit/river application distinction. The wording ambiguity around salt and plaster must remain a debt; resolving it by adding an unowned branch would invalidate the source account.
dependencies: SAND_SAMPLE and application registers are source-side abstractions; no target word or manuscript operator is assigned.
The shared FIT_MORTAR judgment is source-attested, while modern material science explanations are excluded.
The accessible English translation's repeated pit-sand wording in the salt/plaster passage is preserved as unresolved; no silent correction is imported from another edition.
The complete source scope is Book II chapter 4 only; Book II chapter 5 ratios and later material chapters are not used to repair this card.
access: No Voynich target rows, images, reserves, f84/f84r/f116v, root experiment files, route, ledger, or frozen source packet were opened or changed.
